artifactEvidence.excerpt: A September 4 paper in Nature Communications reports an AI system that predicts later liver spread after stomach-cancer surgery. It studied 1,878 people with cancer that had spread into nearby tissue or lymph nodes, called locally advanced cancer. In these records, combining image patterns and clinical information outperformed clinical information alone at distinguishing those who later had liver spread from those who did not.

A model is a learned system that turns information into a prediction. This one combines pre-surgery CT scans—detailed internal images—with microscope images of tissue removed during surgery and clinical details. The team used some patients’ records and known later outcomes to learn which combinations went with later liver spread, then checked the prediction on separate patient groups.

readerValue.reason: Beyond the headline, the reader gains the prediction-vs-benefit distinction and concrete questions to ask about any health-AI claim.

explainBack.question: Why can a model that accurately predicts which patients will later have liver spread still fail to help patients, causally speaking?
explainBack.answer: The model learned statistical associations between past patients' scans, tissue images and clinical details and their known later outcomes, then had those associations checked on separate patient groups. That establishes only that the score sorts risk in similar records. Helping patients requires a further causal step: someone must change a decision — surveillance frequency, added therapy — because of the score, and that changed decision must itself cause better outcomes. If clinicians act on a false alarm, the intervention's harms arrive without the predicted event; if a missed warning breeds reassurance, care may be withheld from someone who needed it. Neither effect is measurable from the prediction study, because no care was assigned using the score.
explainBack.expectedEvidence: A correct answer must distinguish learning from labelled historical outcomes (P003, P012) from an interventional test of score-guided care, note that the reused trial assigned chemotherapy, not the AI (P005), and cite the false-alarm/missed-warning consequence chain (P008) and the explicit absence of an outcome test (P010).
explainBack.assessment: The article fully supports this causal answer: every link — labelled training, separate-group checking, trial reuse, error consequences, and the missing outcome trial — is stated in the artifact in ordinary language.

unseenTransfer.scenario: A city's fire department buys an AI that analyses building inspection records, wiring age and past call-outs, and it accurately flags which apartment blocks are most likely to have a serious fire in the next two years. A councillor proposes cutting the fire-prevention budget because 'the AI now protects those buildings.'
unseenTransfer.question: Using the article's mechanism, what is wrong with the councillor's reasoning, and what evidence would justify confidence that the AI is protecting residents?
unseenTransfer.answer: The AI has only demonstrated the first of two separate questions: it identifies risk from labelled past examples. Nothing yet shows that acting on its flags — reinspections, retrofits, tenant warnings — actually reduces fires, nor which actions work. A false alarm could force costly evacuations or retrofits on safe buildings; a missed flag could leave a dangerous block with reduced prevention coverage precisely because the budget was cut. Justified confidence requires evidence about the intervention: a comparison in which flagged buildings receiving AI-guided prevention are measured for actual fire outcomes against comparable buildings under standard practice, with testing representative of the real building stock and of how inspectors use the scores in their workflow.
unseenTransfer.expectedEvidence: Application of the P004 two-question split, the P008 false-alarm/missed-warning error consequences, and the P007 human-AI-team-in-real-setting evaluation standard to a domain absent from the article.
unseenTransfer.assessment: The transfer succeeds: the article's mechanism resolves the scenario completely without extra concepts, confirming the explanation teaches a portable model rather than a story about one paper.
